title: Proving with vectors
objectives: Use vectors to show that points lie on a line or that lines are parallel.
Prove a geometric fact by writing every side in terms of two vectors.

screens.prose: Three points: $A(1, 1)$, $B(3, 2)$ and $C(7, 4)$. The arrows $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ both start at A.
screens.question: Does C lie on the straight line through A and B?

options.why: Length does not decide it. A longer arrow can lie along the same line.

options.text: Yes, because C is further right than B
options.why: Being further right is not enough. $(7, 6)$ is further right too, and it is off the line.

options.text: We cannot tell without a ruler
options.why: The components decide it exactly. Compare $\overrightarrow{AC}$ with $\overrightarrow{AB}$.

hints.text: $(6, 3) = 3 \times (2, 1)$. Both arrows leave A in the same direction.

feedback.correct: Same direction from the same point.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare the two arrows as columns.

byKey.longer: You judged by length. Two arrows from A in the same direction lie on one line, whatever their lengths.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{AC} = (6, 3) = 3(2, 1) = 3\overrightarrow{AB}$. So both arrows leave A in the same direction. A point reached from A in that direction is on the line through A and B.

screens.prose: The shaded line holds every multiple of $\mathbf{u} = \begin{pmatrix} 2 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix}$. Drag the head of $\mathbf{v}$ around. The caption divides each component of $\mathbf{v}$ by the matching one of $\mathbf{u}$.
screens.question: When does the head of $\mathbf{v}$ sit on the shaded line?

options.text: When the two quotients are equal

options.why: Try $(4, 4)$. It is longer than u but off the line.

options.text: When the two components of v are equal
options.why: Try $(2, 2)$. Its components match, but it is off the line.

options.text: When both components of v are positive
options.why: Try $(-4, -2)$. Both are negative, and it sits on the line.

feedback.correct: One number k works in both rows.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Drag v onto the line and compare the two quotients.

explain.text: On the line both quotients equal the same k, so $\mathbf{v} = k\mathbf{u}$. Off the line they differ, and no single k works. That test is exact, so it can prove things.

screens.prose: Points are **collinear** when one straight line passes through them all. To prove it, show $\overrightarrow{AC} = k\overrightarrow{AB}$: parallel arrows from the same point A. Try $A(2, 1)$, $B(4, 4)$ and $C(8, 10)$.
screens.question: Find the number $k$ with $\overrightarrow{AC} = k\overrightarrow{AB}$.

hints.text: Write $\overrightarrow{AB}$ and $\overrightarrow{AC}$ as columns, end minus start.

feedback.correct: The same k in both rows, so A, B and C are collinear.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find both vectors from A, then divide row by row.

byKey.bc: That compares $\overrightarrow{BC}$ $= (4, 6)$ with $\overrightarrow{AB}$. Both arrows here must start at A.
byKey.positions: You divided the position of C by the position of B. Use the vectors from A.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{AC} = (6, 9) = 3(2, 3) = 3\overrightarrow{AB}$. The arrows are parallel and share the point A, so they lie on one line. A, B and C are collinear, with C three times as far from A as B.

screens.prose: New points: $A(0, 1)$, $B(2, 2)$ and $C(6, 5)$. They look close to a line on the diagram.
screens.question: Are A, B and C collinear?

options.text: No: the two rows need different values of $k$
Yes: both arrows point up and to the right
options.why: Many directions point up and to the right. The test is one k for both rows.
Only the top row triples. The bottom row goes from 1 to 4, which is 4 times.

options.text: Yes: they are close enough to a line
options.why: A proof needs exact equality. Close is not collinear.

hints.text: Write both vectors from A as columns.

feedback.correct: 3 in one row and 4 in the other, so no single k.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide row by row and compare.

byKey.three: You checked only the top row. The bottom row needs $k = 4$, so the arrows are not parallel.

explain.text: Top row: $6 = 3 \times 2$. Bottom row: $4 = 4 \times 1$. No single k works, so the arrows point different ways. C is off the line through A and B.

screens.prose: Triangle OAB has $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$. M is the midpoint of OA and N is the midpoint of OB.
screens.question: Which expression is $\overrightarrow{MN}$?

options.why: That is start minus end, the move from N back to M.
That is $\overrightarrow{AB}$, the whole side. M and N are only halfway out.
You added the halves. To go from M to N you first go back to O.

hints.text: Route the trip through O: from M back to O, then out to N.

feedback.correct: Back half of $\mathbf{a}$, then out half of $\mathbf{b}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Go from M to O, then from O to N.

byKey.back: You took start minus end. M to N is $\overrightarrow{ON} - \overrightarrow{OM}$.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{MN} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{b} = \tfrac{1}{2}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$. On the diagram, $\mathbf{a} = (6, 2)$ and $\mathbf{b} = (2, 4)$, so $\overrightarrow{MN} = (-2, 1)$. Compare it with $\overrightarrow{AB} = (-4, 2)$.

screens.question: Do A, B, C and D all lie on one line?

options.text: No: the two arrows are parallel but on different lines

options.why: That proves the arrows are parallel. Parallel lines can sit side by side without meeting.

options.text: No: $\overrightarrow{CD}$ is twice as long as $\overrightarrow{AB}$
options.why: Length is not the reason. A longer arrow can lie on the same line.
We can: test a vector that joins the two arrows, such as $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

hints.text: Parallel is one condition. What else does collinear need?
Is C on the line through A and B? Test $\overrightarrow{AC}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check whether the two arrows share a line, not just a direction.

byKey.yes: You treated parallel as the same line. Parallel arrows can lie on two separate lines, as these do.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{CD} = 2\overrightarrow{AB}$ makes the lines parallel. But $\overrightarrow{AC} = (0, 2)$ is not a multiple of $(2, 1)$, so C is off line AB. Collinear needs parallel arrows that share a point.

screens.prose: Two tests cover everything you did. **Parallel:** $\mathbf{v} = k\mathbf{u}$ for one scalar $k$. **Collinear:** $\overrightarrow{PR} = k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$, parallel arrows from a shared point P.
screens.question: Which fact proves that P, Q and R are collinear?

options.why: Lengths alone say nothing about direction. R could be anywhere on a circle round P.
That needs a shared point too. And S is not one of the three points.
That puts R on the line through the origin and Q. P need not be on it.

feedback.correct: Parallel arrows from the shared point P.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The test needs a direction and a shared point.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{PR} = 4\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$ says R lies in the direction of Q, seen from P. Both arrows start at P, so P, Q and R share one line.

screens.prose: Prove the midpoint result for any triangle OAB, with M and N the midpoints of OA and OB.
screens.question: Put the lines of the proof in order.

lines.text: $\overrightarrow{MN} = \overrightarrow{MO} + \overrightarrow{ON}$, going from M to N by way of O
$= -\tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathbf{b}$, since M and N are halfway along $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$
So MN is parallel to AB and half its length, because it is a scalar multiple of it

hints.text: Start by choosing a route from M to N.
Then write each piece in terms of $\mathbf{a}$ and $\mathbf{b}$.
Route, substitute, factorise, recognise AB, conclude.

feedback.correct: Each line rests on the one before.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start with a route from M to N and finish with the conclusion.

byKey.s5: The conclusion comes last, once MN is a multiple of AB.
byKey.s4: You can name AB only once $\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}$ appears.

explain.text: The proof never used the shape of the triangle. So in every triangle, the line joining two midpoints is parallel to the third side and half as long.

screens.prose: A stock closes at $\text{£}100.00$ on day 0, $\text{£}104.50$ on day 3 and $\text{£}110.50$ on day 7. Plot each close as a point (day, price): P, Q and R. A steady trend means the points are collinear.
screens.question: Find $k$ with $\overrightarrow{QR} = k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$, to two decimal places.

hints.text: Write both vectors as (days, change in £).

feedback.correct: $\tfrac{4}{3}$ in both rows: a steady trend.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide QR by PQ row by row.

byKey.inverse: You divided PQ by QR. We want the k that turns $\overrightarrow{PQ}$ into $\overrightarrow{QR}$.
byKey.price: You divided the prices, $110.50 \div 104.50$. Use the changes, not the levels.
byKey.days: You divided the day numbers, 7 by 3. Use the gaps between days, 4 and 3.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{QR} = (4, 6.00) = \tfrac{4}{3}(3, 4.50) = \tfrac{4}{3}\overrightarrow{PQ}$. The arrows share Q, so P, Q and R are collinear. The price rises a steady $\text{£}1.50$ a day.

ideas: Two vectors are parallel when one is a scalar multiple of the other, with one k for both rows.
Three points are collinear when $\overrightarrow{PR} = k\,\overrightarrow{PQ}$: parallel arrows from a shared point.
To prove a fact about a shape, write every side in terms of two vectors and simplify.

formula.name: Collinear points
formula.note: Parallel alone is not enough: the arrows must share a point.

summary.trap: Parallel arrows can lie on two separate lines. Collinear needs a shared point as well.

quiz.prose: In triangle OAB, $\overrightarrow{OA} = \mathbf{a}$ and $\overrightarrow{OB} = \mathbf{b}$. P lies on AB with $\overrightarrow{AP} = \tfrac{1}{4}\overrightarrow{AB}$.
quiz.question: Which expression is $\overrightarrow{OP}$?

options.why: That point is a quarter of the way from B, not from A.
You used $\tfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{b}$ for the step along AB. That step is $\tfrac{1}{4}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a})$.
You scaled the sum. Go to A first, then a quarter of the way to B.

explain.text: $\overrightarrow{OP} = \mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{4}(\mathbf{b} - \mathbf{a}) = \tfrac{3}{4}\mathbf{a} + \tfrac{1}{4}\mathbf{b}$. P sits closer to A, so a carries the larger weight.
